objective: Predict, then fix, five real IAM evaluation puzzles: an explicit Deny, a permission boundary, an SCP region lock, an MFA condition, and a cross-account bucket policy that needs TLS.
successCriteria: You predicted allow/deny correctly for an explicit-Deny case and a permission-boundary case before fixing anything
You wrote an explicit Deny, a boundary, an SCP, an MFA-conditioned Deny and a bucket policy that all pass their behaviour tests
You can explain why Deny wins, why boundaries and SCPs never grant, and why cross-account access needs both sides to allow
hints: IAM starts at default deny, then looks for an explicit Deny anywhere. Only if there is none does it look for an Allow that every guardrail also permits.
Boundaries and SCPs only cap permissions; they never grant. A Deny that uses NotAction lets you carve out exceptions without enumerating everything you block.

For MFA use a Deny with BoolIfExists aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent=false (so a missing key is denied too). For the bucket: name the partner role as Principal, include BOTH the bucket ARN and bucket/* in Resource, and add a Deny on Bool aws:SecureTransport=false.

range.scenario: You have just joined the cloud platform team at Acme (account 111122223333) and the on-call queue is full of access tickets that all come down to one question: what will IAM actually decide? A contractor must not delete production ledgers, a build bot has an admin policy it should never have been trusted with, the Organization needs a region lock, ops want MFA on destructive calls, and a partner needs read access to a bucket. For each ticket you first PREDICT the verdict, then FIX the policy and let the evaluator check your reasoning. Use the terminal to run the IAM policy simulator against real users.

tasks.prompt: Predict first. Read contractor-sam-policy.json. Can contractor-sam call s3:DeleteObject on arn:aws:s3:::acme-prod-ledger/2026/q3.csv?
options: Yes: the Allow on s3:* matches, and an Allow is all that is needed
No: the explicit Deny matches the request, and an explicit Deny beats every Allow
Yes: the Allow statement is listed first, and IAM stops at the first match
No, but only because a bucket policy must also be present to allow it
tasks.explanation: IAM does not read statements in order and does not stop at the first match. It collects every matching statement, and a single matching explicit Deny ends the evaluation with deny, no matter how many Allows also match. That is why Deny is the tool for 'never, under any circumstances' rules.

tasks.prompt: Verify your prediction in the terminal: simulate s3:DeleteObject on arn:aws:s3:::acme-prod-ledger/2026/q3.csv for contractor-sam. What is the EvalDecision value?
tasks.explanation: The simulator reports explicitDeny (a Deny statement matched) rather than implicitDeny (nothing allowed it). The difference matters when debugging: an explicitDeny means you must find and change the Deny, because adding more Allows can never fix it.

tasks.prompt: Ticket 1: fix ravi's policy (ravi-policy.json). He must keep full S3 access to the staging ledger and still list and read the prod ledger, but he must NOT be able to delete objects, delete object versions or upload (overwrite) objects in prod.

tests.name: Can still read prod ledger objects
Can still list the prod ledger bucket
Cannot delete prod ledger objects
Cannot delete prod object versions
Cannot overwrite prod ledger objects
Can still upload to staging
Can still delete from staging

tasks.explanation: Instead of untangling a broad Allow, add an explicit Deny scoped to the prod objects. Because Deny wins over any Allow, ravi keeps his wide staging rights, reads in prod still work (they are not denied), and writes in prod are blocked even if someone later adds another Allow.

tasks.prompt: Predict first. BuildBot's identity policy (buildbot-identity-policy.json) allows * on *. Its permissions boundary allows only s3:*, dynamodb:*, logs:* and cloudwatch:*. Can BuildBot call iam:CreateUser?
options: Yes: the identity policy allows everything, and the boundary only restricts what you can grant
No: an action must be allowed by BOTH the identity policy and the boundary, and the boundary has no iam allow
Yes: boundaries only apply to IAM users, not roles
No: boundaries remove only the actions they explicitly list
tasks.explanation: A permission boundary is a cap, not a grant: the effective permission is the intersection of the identity policy and the boundary. An admin policy under a narrow boundary can do only what the boundary allows. Boundaries work as an allow-list, they do not list 'denied' actions.

tasks.prompt: Ticket 2: write the permissions boundary for BuildBot (the draft is in buildbot-boundary-draft.json; the admin identity policy is fixed and cannot change). BuildBot may use S3, DynamoDB, CloudWatch Logs and CloudWatch only. IAM and everything else must be out of reach even though its identity policy says *.

tests.name: Can read S3 objects
Can write DynamoDB items
Can write CloudWatch Logs
Cannot create IAM users despite the admin policy
Cannot attach policies to roles
Cannot launch EC2 instances

tasks.explanation: The draft boundary allowed iam:*, which silently re-opened the most dangerous service (a role that can edit IAM can remove its own boundary or mint new admins). A boundary should be a tight allow-list. Anything not listed is denied, no matter how broad the identity policy is.

tasks.prompt: Predict first. region-lock-scp-draft.json denies Action * unless aws:RequestedRegion is eu-west-1 or eu-central-1. An engineer in the Organization (admin identity policy) runs iam:CreateRole. IAM is a global service whose requests are served from us-east-1. What happens?
options: Allowed: IAM is global, so SCP region conditions are ignored
Denied: the request region is us-east-1, so the blanket Deny matches and IAM, STS and other global services break too
Allowed: SCPs never apply to administrators
Denied only for the management account
tasks.explanation: A blanket region Deny also hits global services, which are called with a region of us-east-1. Real region-lock SCPs therefore use NotAction to exempt global services (iam, sts, organizations, route53, support, cloudfront, budgets...) so the lock only bites regional services.

tasks.prompt: Ticket 3: fix the region-lock SCP (region-lock-scp-draft.json). A fixed FullAWSAccess allow SCP and an admin identity policy are already in place. Regional services must work only in eu-west-1 and eu-central-1; global services such as IAM and STS must keep working.

tests.name: Can launch EC2 in eu-west-1
Can create S3 buckets in eu-central-1
Cannot launch EC2 in us-east-1
Cannot create S3 buckets in ap-south-1
Global IAM still works (served from us-east-1)
STS still works from us-east-1

tasks.explanation: SCPs never grant, so the FullAWSAccess allow is what keeps everything permitted and your SCP only adds a Deny on top. Using NotAction for the global services means 'deny everything except these' under the region condition. A condition-based Deny in an SCP is the standard way to enforce data-residency.

tasks.prompt: Ticket 4: harden ops-engineer-policy.json. ec2:StopInstances, ec2:TerminateInstances and rds:DeleteDBInstance must work only in an MFA-authenticated session. Sessions from a plain access key do not carry aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent at all, and they must still be able to describe instances.

tests.name: Can describe instances without MFA (key is absent from the request)
Can terminate instances in an MFA session
Cannot terminate instances when MFA is explicitly false
Cannot terminate instances from a long-term key (no MFA key at all)
Cannot delete databases without MFA
Can delete databases in an MFA session

tasks.explanation: Use a Deny with BoolIfExists aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent=false. Plain Bool would not match when the key is missing (long-term access keys never carry it), so those sessions would slip through. IfExists makes the missing key count as a match, so the Deny covers both 'false' and 'absent'.

tasks.prompt: Ticket 5: write the bucket policy for acme-partner-reports (draft in partner-bucket-policy-draft.json). The caller's own identity policy already allows s3:* (fixed) and this is a CROSS-ACCOUNT request. Only role arn:aws:iam::444455556666:role/PartnerAnalytics may call s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket, and every request over plain HTTP must be refused for everyone.

tests.name: Partner can read reports over HTTPS
Partner can list the bucket over HTTPS
Partner is refused over plain HTTP
An unrelated account cannot read reports
Partner cannot upload or overwrite reports

tasks.explanation: Across accounts both sides must allow: the caller's identity policy AND the bucket policy that names the caller. Principal * in the draft let every account in, and Resource listed only bucket/*, so ListBucket (which targets the bucket ARN itself) never matched. The TLS rule is an explicit Deny on aws:SecureTransport=false, which wins over any Allow.

takeaways: Evaluation order: explicit Deny anywhere wins; then SCPs and permission boundaries must allow (they only cap); then an identity or resource Allow grants. No match means implicit deny.
Use explicit Deny for 'never' rules, and BoolIfExists / NotAction patterns so a missing condition key or a global service does not create a loophole.
Cross-account access needs two yeses (caller's identity policy and the resource policy), and S3 bucket-level actions like ListBucket need the bucket ARN as well as bucket/*.

objective: Assume a cross-account role with the AWS CLI (using an ExternalId), switch to the temporary credentials, prove what the assumed identity can and cannot do, then fix an over-broad role trust policy.
successCriteria: You assumed AuditReaderRole, exported all three temporary credential values and confirmed the assumed-role identity
You read the audit report using the temporary credentials and showed that the role cannot write or delete
You rewrote a trust policy so only the intended principal with the correct ExternalId can assume the role
hints: Start with `aws sts get-caller-identity`, then try the bucket. The access denied tells you which identity is calling. Look at the role's trust policy artifact for what the role demands from callers.

AssumeRole returns three secrets: AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey and SessionToken. Export all three as AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY and AWS_SESSION_TOKEN, then call get-caller-identity again.

aws sts assume-role --role-arn arn:aws:iam::444455556666:role/AuditReaderRole --role-session-name audit-lab --external-id tz-audit-7f3c. For the trust policy, copy the structure of the working AuditReaderRole trust: a specific Principal plus a StringEquals sts:ExternalId condition.

tasks.prompt: AssumeRole returns a set of temporary credentials. To make the AWS CLI act as the role, which values must you export?
options: Only AccessKeyId, like a normal IAM user key
AccessKeyId and SecretAccessKey, the SessionToken is optional
AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey and SessionToken
Only the SessionToken, it replaces the key pair
tasks.explanation: Temporary credentials are a triple. The SessionToken is what proves the key pair is a live STS session, and requests signed with just the key and secret are rejected (InvalidClientTokenId). Forgetting AWS_SESSION_TOKEN is the most common reason an assumed role 'does not work'.

tasks.prompt: Run the round trip in the terminal. After exporting the temporary credentials, `aws sts get-caller-identity` shows a different identity. What is the full Arn it returns?
tasks.explanation: The caller is no longer the user deploy-bot but an assumed-role session: arn:aws:sts::<role account>:assumed-role/<role>/<session name>. The account is the ROLE's account (444455556666), and the session name you chose is what appears in CloudTrail, so a descriptive name makes later investigations much easier.

tasks.prompt: Using the assumed-role credentials, read s3://acme-audit-reports/q3-findings.txt (print it with `aws s3 cp ... -`). Paste the flag from the report.
tasks.explanation: As deploy-bot the bucket was AccessDenied: that user holds no S3 permission at all. After AssumeRole the CLI acts as AuditReaderRole, whose permission policy allows reading the bucket. The trust policy decided who could become the role; the permission policy decided what the role can do.

tasks.prompt: While using the temporary credentials you try `aws s3 rm` on the report and get AccessDenied. What is the best explanation?
options: The temporary credentials have already expired, so every call is rejected
An assumed-role session has only the role's permissions (here read-only); deploy-bot's own permissions no longer apply
S3 never allows deletes from the CLI
The ExternalId must be passed again on every call
tasks.explanation: When you assume a role you give up your original permissions and get exactly the role's, nothing more. AuditReaderRole's policy grants only s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket, so a delete is denied and the failure message names the assumed-role ARN as the caller. This is least privilege working as intended.

tasks.prompt: If you do not pass --duration-seconds, how long (in seconds) are the temporary credentials from sts:AssumeRole valid by default?
tasks.explanation: The AssumeRole default is 3600 seconds (one hour). The valid range runs from 900 seconds up to the role's configured maximum (1 to 12 hours). Short lifetimes are a major advantage of roles over long-term keys: a stolen session simply stops working.

tasks.prompt: Wear Northwind's hat. Harden the trust policy of the new ComplianceExportRole (draft in ComplianceExportRole-trust-draft.json). Only IAM user arn:aws:iam::111122223333:user/deploy-bot may assume it, and only when it presents ExternalId tz-export-91ac. Callers' own identity policies already allow sts:AssumeRole (fixed), and the request is cross-account.

tests.name: deploy-bot can assume the role with the correct ExternalId
deploy-bot cannot assume the role without any ExternalId
deploy-bot cannot assume the role with a wrong ExternalId
A role in an unrelated account cannot assume it, even with the right ExternalId
An anonymous caller cannot assume it

tasks.explanation: Principal * with no condition means any AWS principal in any account that learns the role ARN can assume it. The fix has two parts: name the exact principal, and require sts:ExternalId so a different customer of the same vendor cannot trick the vendor into assuming your role on their behalf (the confused deputy problem).

tasks.prompt: What attack does an ExternalId condition in a role trust policy primarily defend against?
options: Brute-forcing the role's session token
The confused deputy problem: a third party being tricked into assuming a customer's role for someone else
Man-in-the-middle attacks on the STS endpoint
Replay of an expired session after the role is deleted
tasks.explanation: A vendor serves many customers from one AWS account. Without a per-customer ExternalId, customer B could give the vendor customer A's role ARN and have the vendor assume it. The ExternalId is a per-customer value that only the real relationship knows, so the trust policy rejects the substituted request. It is not a secret key and does not encrypt anything.

takeaways: AssumeRole trades your identity for a time-limited one: export AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey and SessionToken, and from then on you have only the role's permissions.

Two documents gate a role: the trust policy decides who may assume it, and the permission policy decides what the session can do. Cross-account assumption needs the caller's identity policy and the trust policy to both allow.
Never trust Principal * in a trust policy; name the exact principal and add sts:ExternalId for third-party access to prevent confused-deputy abuse.
